metadata.title: TSMC Has a 'Substantially Wider Moat' Than Nvidia, Says Investor Joseph Carlson

content.text:
Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.
Investor Joseph Carlson has bought $30,000 of TSMC (NYSE:TSM) and plans to invest another $30,000 if the stock falls further, believing the chipmaker has a stronger competitive position than Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).
"I think that TSM has a substantially wider moat than even the likes of Nvidia or AMD," Carlson said on his YouTube show Monday.
Why TSMC Sits Above Nvidia
Carlson considered several beaten-down AI stocks, including Nvidia, AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) and Micron, before settling on TSMC.
He ranks ASML Holding NV (NASDAQ:ASML), which dominates the market for advanced lithography equipment used to make chips, at the top of the semiconductor supply chain, followed by TSMC and then chip designers such as Nvidia and AMD.
He already owns ASML but believes TSMC offers better value because it trades at a considerably lower earnings multiple.
Competing with TSMC, he argues, requires enormous investment, technical expertise and the ability to manufacture advanced chips at scale.
TSMC accounted for 72.5% of global contract chipmaking revenue in the second quarter, compared with 5.9% for its nearest competitor, Samsung, according to TrendForce research.
TSMC can also benefit from growing competition between its customers. While Nvidia faces competition from AMD and cloud computing companies designing their own AI chips, TSMC manufactures chips for them all. "TSM is a layer above these companies," Carlson said.
Buying Into the Panic
TSMC shares have fallen about 28% from their October peak, despite the company's October revenue rising 59.7% year over year in local currency. Carlson attributes the sell-off to political uncertainty and Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia rather than deteriorating fundamentals.
He had intended to buy between $315 and $330 but went ahead at around $360 after Huang's reinstatement lifted semiconductor stocks Monday. TSMC gave back some of those gains Tuesday, closing at $349.20, below Carlson's purchase price.
His $450 fair value estimate implies nearly 29% upside from Tuesday's close, and he believes TSMC can get there even if analysts don't raise their earnings forecasts.
Prediction Traders See Trouble Ahead
Competition among its customers may help TSMC, but a broader slowdown in AI spending could hurt them all.
Traders on Polymarket put the odds of the AI bubble bursting by year-end at 35%, with $3.62 million traded. That rises to 52% by June 2027.
Three of the contract's six conditions, which include a 50% decline in Nvidia shares or a 40% decline in a major semiconductor ETF from their record highs, must occur within 90 days.
